chronicle.text: 8 settlers land on Hais and light a fire.
Vidor wades into the shallows with a sharpened stick and comes back with fish. Hais learns to fish.
Saaris lays a timber floor on four posts and heaps the grain on it, out of the damp. Hais learns to build granaries.
The first granary stands on Hais, its floor raised above the damp.
Saaris watches the clouds pile up over the sea and says the gentle days are over. From now on the sky brings rain, storms, heat and hard frost.
Saaris finds great paw prints in the mud and hears howling from the deep woods. Wolves live on Hais, and boars root among the trees.
Saaris lashes a flint point to a long ash pole. If the beasts come for Hais, Hais will go out after them. The islanders learn to hunt.
Boars root through 3 fields by the woods in the night. The grain is trampled and torn up. Nobody on Hais has an answer for them yet.
Vidor and Duten spear a boar in its wallow and carry it home. The first boar taken on Hais; there is roast pork at the fire tonight.
Saaris says the longest day should not pass like any other. On midsummer evening the work will stop, the fire will be built high, and all of Hais will dance around it.
At first light Saaris sees four deer grazing on the open grass east of the village. They lift their heads, stare, and are gone into the trees. Not everything in the woods of Hais has teeth.
Midsummer on Hais: 9 people dance around a towering bonfire and feast on the best of the stores. The first midsummer fire on Hais burns until nearly midnight.
Saaris drives a row of stakes along the trampled grain and weaves hazel rods between them. Hais learns to fence its fields.
Racemor ties off the last hazel rod. The first fence on Hais stands between the grain and the woods.
Boars snuffle along the new fences all night and find no way in. In the morning the grain stands untouched.

A wall of grey rolls in off the sea and swallows Hais. From the beach Saaris cannot see the water, and from the fields nobody can see the trees. Nobody fishes and nobody hunts, and somewhere out in the white a wolf howls in broad day.
Vidor and Duten creep up through the long grass downwind and bring down a deer. The first venison on Hais; the hide is pegged out to dry and the bones are kept for needles.
A wolf leaps on Vidor out of the fog. She limps home, badly bitten. For weeks after, nobody stays out past dusk.
The grass between the hearth and the beach is trodden down to bare earth. Nobody laid it out; the feet of Hais did. Saaris notices the walk is quicker on it, and the others follow the track.
Vidor and Duten track the pack to its den and kill a wolf. Its pelt will hang by the fire. The first wolf ever slain on Hais.

Saaris walks out to a quiet patch of ground north of the village and sets a ring of stones there. Arys is laid in the earth inside it, and 3 mourners stand at the graveside next morning. Hais has a burying ground.
Hais is home to 10 people.
Wenra, the first child born on Hais, arrives to Seran and Morceem.
Wolves take Saaris in the fog. Nobody saw them come. Hais learns to fear the dark woods. For weeks after, nobody stays out past dusk.
Four days of fog lift. Out of the grey, wolves took one of the village.

The wolves come out of the fog, and nobody hears them until it is too late. Morceem brings up a great whelk shell from the beach, knocks off its tip and blows: a low moan rolls out over the fields and into the trees. On fog days now someone keeps by the hearth and blows the horn, and whoever can hear it can call back. Hais has a fog horn.

A raft of lashed logs drifts onto the beach with nobody aboard but three goats, thin and bleating. Morceem wades out and leads them ashore, and by nightfall a wattle pen stands beside the village. Morceem takes a crook and goes out with them each morning. Hais keeps goats.

Hamor comes in from the edge of the woods with a wolf cub in her arms, thin and shivering; it had crept out of the den alone. The grown-ups argue half the night about knocking it on the head. In the end it stays: Hamor calls him Cull, feeds him fish heads and lets him sleep across the doorway. Cull grows up thinking the village is his pack. Hais has a dog.

Something has been at the grain: husks strewn over the granary floor, droppings in the chaff, a little trail worn into the grass. At dusk Morceem sees a grey shape run along the granary beam and drop into the heap. Rats have come to Hais, and nobody knows how they came ashore.

On midsummer day Morceem sees a dugout come in over the sea with 3 strangers at the paddles. They come from an isle beyond the haze, where the midsummer fires of Hais have been seen. Their words are strange, but they have come for the dance. Hais is not alone in the sea.
A week of storms batters Hais: 1 roof torn away, 2 fences blown down.

The rats have multiplied past counting. At night the granary floor seethes, they run along the rafters and squeal in the thatch, and Emser wakes screaming with one on the blanket. Whatever grain they do not eat, they foul.

A wolf tears through the back of the goat pen in the night and drags off a kid. Nobody wakes until it is over; in the morning there is a hole in the wattle and a red trail across the snow. The winter woods are empty, and the wolves have found the goat pen.

The nights are long and black, and Morceem, the eldest, says the old days must not be forgotten. On the longest night all of Hais sits close round the hearth, the children in front, and Morceem tells of the fog: how it comes in off the sea without a sound, how a child who strays past the last house cannot find the way back, and how the wolves walk in it by day. Saaris went out into it and did not come home. Nobody fidgets. Since that night the children of Hais keep close to the houses when the fog comes in. From now on a tale is told every year on the longest night.
Vidor carries home her tenth kill. The children play at being Vidor the Hunter now, with sticks for spears.
A fever comes to Hais. The boat from the far isle is hardly out of sight when Racemor begins to shiver. Nobody on Hais has seen its like, and nobody knows what to do but keep the fire going and wait.
